logline: A struggling manga artist with the involuntary power to rewind time moments before disasters finds himself hurled eighteen years into the past - his only chance to stop a childhood serial killer and save his own mother.

renewal.note: Single 12-episode season adapting Kei Sanbe's manga in full. Aired January to March 2016 on Fuji TV's Noitamina block. A separate Netflix live-action adaptation was released in December 2017.

bollymeter.basis: A 100% Tomatometer from 6 critics and a 95% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes confirm near-universal acclaim; the series is widely cited as one of the tightest thriller anime produced in the 2010s, with its compressed 12-episode structure praised for eliminating filler.

seasons.review_body: Broadcast on Fuji TV's prestige Noitamina block from January to March 2016, Erased arrived with an unusually clean concept: time travel as a procedural device for childhood trauma investigation. A-1 Pictures executed it with formal economy. The 12-episode limit, which could have felt rushed, instead functioned as a structural discipline - every episode advanced both timelines and the mystery tightened rather than sprawled. Rotten Tomatoes registered 100 percent from the critics who reviewed it, with the audience score at 95 percent. Available on Netflix internationally.

episode_reviews.title: Flashing Before My Eyes
episode_reviews.review_body: Erased's premiere aired January 8, 2016 on Fuji TV's prestige Noitamina block and established the series' core grammar in under twenty minutes. Satoru Fujinuma's Revival ability - which forces him back in time whenever someone near him is about to die - is introduced and deployed at full narrative stakes without a single expository detour. A-1 Pictures made the decision to render the adult 2006 timeline in muted, washed palette and the childhood 1988 sequences in warmer, more saturated tones, a formal choice that the premiere established and the series never abandoned. Rotten Tomatoes registered 100 percent approval from the initial wave of critics on the series, and the premiere's structural clarity - two timelines, one mechanism, no wasted minutes - was cited as evidence that the twelve-episode limit would be an asset rather than a constraint. The series landed on Netflix internationally as one of A-1 Pictures' strongest offerings of the decade.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere introduces Satoru's Revival ability with the minimum of exposition and immediately deploys it at full stakes. The tonal blend of mundane adult anxiety and supernatural thriller mechanics clicks into place with unusual speed for an anime premiere.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The first Revival sequence - the show announces its grammar in seconds and never has to explain itself again.

episode_reviews.title: It's Okay
episode_reviews.review_body: Erased Episode 7 'It's Okay' was the episode that consolidated the series' reputation as the best anime of the Noitamina Winter 2016 block and one of the strongest A-1 Pictures productions of the decade. The episode centres the relationship between Satoru and Kayo - the child the series had positioned as the primary victim of the killer the adult timeline is trying to identify - and writer Taku Kishimoto handled the specific horror of a child in genuine danger with a restraint that most thriller writers refuse. The 95 percent Rotten Tomatoes audience score on the series reflects in large part the accumulated trust this episode built: the show had spent six episodes establishing what was at stake, and Episode 7 honoured that investment by arriving at an emotional register that felt earned rather than manipulated. The direction avoided sensationalism throughout in favour of the specific weight of two people in a kitchen, one of whom has never been treated as worth protecting before.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The episode considered the emotional peak of the series by most viewers, centred on Satoru's relationship with Kayo. The writing and direction handle the specific horror of a child in danger with a restraint that makes the stakes feel genuine rather than manipulative.

episode_reviews.title: Future
episode_reviews.review_body: Erased's finale aired March 25, 2016 and delivered the confrontation between Satoru and the killer that the series had been structuring toward across twelve episodes. Critical reception was characteristically divided on anime finales that carry this weight: viewers who had invested in the mystery's procedural architecture found the resolution satisfying; those who had the emotional arc as their primary investment found the final episode's pacing slightly mechanical. The Rotten Tomatoes audience score of 95 percent on the series overall suggests the dominant response was positive, and the finale's clearest strength is in the parallel timeline resolution - the show had maintained two temporal registers across twelve episodes and closed them with formal economy. The rooftop confrontation was noted by multiple critics as the series' clearest thematic statement about the cost of changing the past when the person doing the changing has lived forward through time while the world stayed frozen.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale resolves both timelines and delivers the confrontation the series has been building toward. Reception was split on how fully the emotional resolution earned the thriller setup, but as a piece of plotting it honours every thread laid in the first act.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The rooftop confrontation - the series' clearest statement about memory, regret, and the price of changing the past.
